summary:
Snapshot 2026-09-26. Google Trends and Wikipedia today are mostly sports and entertainment, with no health breakouts, so the ranking below comes from journal, press and news signals plus our previous snapshots.

Top opportunities:
(1) The BMJ Danish study on HRT pills vs patches and blood clots. It has appeared in all 3 snapshots, now has mainstream coverage, and suits our 25–55 women perfectly.
(2) Three new, low-competition stories picked up in the last 24–48 hours: smartwatch calorie counts off by 15–25% (PLOS One), scented cleaning products creating nanoparticles (ACS), and mammogram overdiagnosis revised to under 5% (JNCI).
(3) Gen X heavy drinking up 36% (Annals of Internal Medicine).
(4) Walking pace vs step count (BJSM).
(5) Topics carried over from earlier snapshots: REM sleep, the SELECT heart-benefit analysis, Galleri, and menopause proteins linked to dementia.

FMT for IBS and the 10-diets study are losing momentum. Flu season is the seasonal driver to watch over the next 2–4 weeks.

Rejected: 'cannabis leaves have medical potential' (lab-only, bait for unproven treatments). Stories on vaccine policy, measles politics and the fentanyl-analog warning were not taken forward. They're off-brand or best left to news outlets.

Minor verification note: the 8,500-steps story is a re-run from May 2026, so it isn't new.

candidates.topic: Menopause HRT pills vs patches/gels and blood clots: ~1 extra serious clot per 1,000 women/year on oral; no overall increase with transdermal (The BMJ, Danish nationwide, 180k+ women)
candidates.angle: 'Pill or patch? The HRT question worth asking your doctor.' Put the absolute risk (1 in 1,000) next to the relative-risk headlines, explain why the liver matters (first-pass effect on clotting factors), and give a list of questions to take to a clinician. Never tell viewers to switch.
candidates.why_now: Seen in 3 consecutive snapshots with momentum climbing (82→86→88). Published Sep 23, now covered by BMJ Group, MedicalXpress, News-Medical and Australian pharmacy press, with expert reactions on Scimex. Menopause is a top interest for our audience, and no big health creator explainer yet.

evidence.signal: Nationwide nested case-control study, Sep 23 2026
Oral linked to higher clot risk regardless of dose or duration; transdermal no overall increase
Mainstream science-news pickup
Independent expert commentary

candidates.topic: Your smartwatch may be off by 15–25% on calories burned, and the error grows with body fat (PLOS One, 4 watches vs metabolic cart)
candidates.angle: 'We tested whether you should eat back your watch calories.' Apple, Garmin, Samsung and Fitbit compared against the lab gold standard. At 35%+ body fat and 4 hours of exercise a week, estimates can be off by 1,200–2,400 kcal/week. Close with what watches ARE good for (steps, heart-rate trends).
keywords: should I eat back exercise calories
candidates.why_now: Posted on MedicalXpress today (Sep 26). Very visual and product-specific, so it tends to spread on TikTok. Only 58 participants, but a clear gold-standard comparison. Almost no creator coverage yet.

evidence.signal: PLOS One study; median error 15–25%; Fitbit readings up to >450% of the measured value

candidates.topic: That 'fresh clean' smell: scented cleaners + indoor ozone create billions of nanoparticles within minutes (Purdue, ACS Fall 2026)
candidates.angle: 'Your cleaning routine might pollute your air more than traffic does.' Explain the terpenes + ozone chemistry in 60 seconds, then 4 fixes: go fragrance-free, open a window, don't stack scented products, and never run ozone/UV-C devices while cleaning. Be clear that the health effects of these tiny particles are still being studied.
candidates.why_now: On ScienceDaily today. Fits the ongoing microplastics/'toxins at home' interest from our earlier snapshots, and comes with practical fixes. Conference data (not a peer-reviewed paper yet), so wording has to be careful.

evidence.signal: Model-home experiments; 10^5–10^8 particles/cm³; exposure can match or exceed standing near heavy traffic

candidates.topic: Mammogram overdiagnosis may be under 5%, not the 30–50% often quoted (JNCI reanalysis of all 8 major RCTs)
candidates.angle: 'The mammogram myth that went the other way.' Explain what overdiagnosis means, why early trial data inflated the estimate (lead-time effects), and what this changes about the screening decision. Frame it as a conversation with your doctor about age and risk. Pair it with the Galleri story as a 'which cancer screens actually work' contrast.
candidates.predicted_peak: 1–2 weeks (October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month)
candidates.why_now: Posted Sep 26 on ScienceDaily and EurekAlert, with small-outlet pickup. Breast Cancer Awareness Month starts in 5 days, which will lift searches. Still debated, so present it as one strong reanalysis, not the final word.

evidence.signal: JNCI meta-analysis; overdiagnosis <5% vs 30–50% earlier estimates
Official press release

candidates.topic: Gen X is drinking more (heavy drinking +36% in ages 50–64) while Gen Z and millennials cut back (Annals of Internal Medicine)
candidates.angle: 'The generation that never got the alcohol memo.' Show the generational split in charts, explain why heavy drinking in midlife matters (liver, cancer risk, sleep, blood pressure), and share evidence-based ways to cut back that don't depend on willpower alone.
keywords: how to cut back on alcohol
candidates.why_now: Guardian, SF Chronicle, NBC and Advisory Board covered it this week. Our audience is 25–55, so both groups are in it. Health creators haven't covered the generational split much.

evidence.signal: Gen X drinking more as younger Americans cut back
Drinking slows after the pandemic spike, mainly among the young
Charts of drinking by generation

candidates.topic: More REM sleep linked to lower risk of 83 diseases (PLOS Medicine, 95,559 UK Biobank wearers)
candidates.angle: 'REM: the sleep stage your tracker keeps nagging you about.' What REM does, why the finding is correlation rather than proof, what cuts REM (alcohol, short sleep, late nights), and the few habits with evidence for protecting it.
keywords: how to get more REM sleep
candidates.why_now: Seen in 3 snapshots, with Inc.com, KSNV and ScienceDaily coverage growing. Sleep is evergreen and this gives it a fresh hook. Links naturally to the Gen X alcohol story.

evidence.signal: More REM sleep linked to lower risk of 83 diseases
Mainstream business/lifestyle pickup

candidates.topic: Weight loss explains only ~20% of semaglutide's heart benefit (SELECT mediation analysis, European Heart Journal)
candidates.angle: 'Ozempic protects hearts, and it's mostly not the weight loss.' Explain mediation analysis simply, the likely pathways (inflammation, blood pressure, direct vascular effects), and what it means for 'thin but at risk' people. No dosing, no 'go get it' messaging.
candidates.why_now: Big trial and a surprising finding, with a companion Diabetes Care paper on predictors of peak weight loss. So far coverage is mostly specialist, so GLP-1 creators have room to explain it.

evidence.signal: Semaglutide and CV risk reduction: SELECT mediation analysis
Predictors of peak weight loss in SELECT

candidates.topic: Walking speed vs step count: fewer than 5,000 fast steps matched 10,000 slow ones for mortality risk (BJSM, 100k+ UK Biobank)
candidates.angle: 'Stop chasing 10,000 steps: pick up the pace instead.' Give the cadence targets (60/80/100 steps per minute) and a 20-second test: count your steps for 15 seconds and multiply by 4. Mention the related 8,500-steps result for keeping weight off, making clear it's from earlier (May).
candidates.why_now: Good Housekeeping, AOL, National Geographic and MNT covering it now. ABC resurfaced the 8,500-steps result today. Easy to act on, which suits Shorts.

evidence.signal: Pace and step count both lower death risk
Recommended cadence thresholds
8,500 steps to keep weight off (meta-analysis of 18 studies)

candidates.topic: Galleri multi-cancer blood test missed its main goal in the 142,942-person NHS RCT, yet an FDA panel still backed it
candidates.angle: 'The $949 cancer blood test: what the big trial actually showed.' Explain what a primary endpoint is (fewer late-stage cancers), false positives, and why an 'advisory panel yes' isn't the same as 'proven to save lives'. Pair with the mammogram story: an established screen with strong evidence vs a new one without it.
candidates.why_now: Seen in 3 snapshots. BMJ news piece Sep 25 on the FDA contradiction. NEJM + Nature Medicine papers. Consumers are actively deciding whether to buy the test.

evidence.signal: Effect of MCED screening on late-stage diagnosis
Galleri fails to meet main aim, but FDA still endorses
Test performance in NHS-Galleri

candidates.topic: Menopause leaves a 16-protein blood 'fingerprint' linked to brain aging and dementia risk (Nature Medicine)
candidates.angle: 'What menopause does to the brain, measured in blood.' Explain the proteomics finding, what it can't yet tell an individual woman, and the dementia risk factors with good evidence behind them (BP, hearing, activity, sleep). Works as a follow-up to the HRT video.
candidates.why_now: 3rd snapshot. MedicalXpress picked it up Sep 25, and it pairs with the HRT story for a menopause series.

evidence.signal: Menopause leaves a fingerprint that may predict dementia risk

candidates.topic: Flu season 2026–27: new mRNA flu shot for 50+, subclade K strain, and 'when should I get it / how long does it last?'
candidates.angle: 'Flu shot timing, explained in 60 seconds.' How long protection lasts, why getting it in October is the usual sweet spot, and what's new this season. Stick strictly to CDC/WHO/NHS guidance and don't touch the policy fights.
keywords: how long does flu shot last
candidates.why_now: Seasonal cycle starting; Detroit Free Press runs 'how long does the flu shot last'. The Roche Xofluza generic-licensing deals add a news hook. Evergreen search demand every October.

evidence.signal: How long does the flu shot last this fall
Generic Xofluza licensing for pandemic preparedness

candidates.topic: Peptides (BPC-157 and others): big promises, thin human evidence, shifting FDA compounding rules
candidates.angle: 'The peptide craze: what's actually been tested in humans?' Separate animal data from human data and explain the gray-market and compounding risks. No sourcing, no dosing, and never present peptides as effective treatments.
candidates.why_now: 2nd snapshot. Outside/Velo ran a 'huge promises, unproven hype' piece Sep 25. Heavy promotion on TikTok and in podcasts, which suits a skeptical explainer.

evidence.signal: Peptides: Huge Promises, Unproven Hype

candidates.topic: Fecal microbiota transplant fails for IBS in phase 3 REFIT2 trial (The Lancet)
candidates.angle: 'The poop transplant that didn't fix IBS, and what does have evidence.' Use it to cut through gut-health hype, then cover what has trial support (low-FODMAP diet with a dietitian, gut-directed CBT/hypnotherapy, fiber types).
candidates.why_now: Strong negative RCT, but momentum is slipping (70→68→62) and pickup is thin. Best as a gut-health evergreen with a fresh hook, not a trend chase.

evidence.signal: REFIT2 randomized double-blind phase 3 trial

candidates.topic: Strokes nearly doubled in adults 20–54 since the 1990s (Neurology)
candidates.angle: 'Stroke isn't an old person's disease anymore.' Cover BE-FAST warning signs, the drivers (blood pressure, diabetes, obesity, drugs), and why young adults delay going to the ER. The life-saving angle is what makes it shareable.
keywords: why are young people having strokes
candidates.why_now: 2nd snapshot. A JAMA Netw Open paper on young adults after stroke and a CBS 'teen's headache' story add to it. Public-service value stays high.

evidence.signal: Antithrombotic therapy and bleeding among young adults after ischemic stroke

candidates.topic: Tirzepatide (Zepbound/Mounjaro) switched on calorie-burning brown fat, but only in obese mice
candidates.angle: 'Does Mounjaro rev your metabolism? Here's what a mouse study can and can't tell you.' Make it a lesson in reading headlines: food intake was matched, so the effect wasn't just eating less, but it's mice only.
candidates.why_now: On ScienceDaily today with a clickbait-friendly headline that GLP-1 creators are likely to overhype. We can be the calm, correct voice.

evidence.signal: Mouse study; food intake matched; researchers caution about applying it to humans

candidates.topic: Vitamin K2 + D3 slowed the rise in coronary calcium scores by 21% (DANCODE RCT, Circulation / ESC 2026)
candidates.angle: 'Can a supplement slow artery calcification?' Explain what CAC scores mean and that a slower-rising score is not proof of fewer heart attacks. Mention the interaction caution: K2 matters for people on warfarin, so talk to a clinician. No dosing.
candidates.why_now: 2nd snapshot. Supplement influencers will latch on, and a measured explainer can rank before the hype.

evidence.signal: DANCODE RCT reported at ESC 2026 / Circulation

candidates.topic: Sleeping with the light on linked to thicker, stiffer hearts (European Heart Journal, 11,071 UK Biobank light sensors)
candidates.angle: 'Your nightlight and your heart.' Cover the link, the circadian mechanism, and cheap fixes (blackout curtains, eye mask, dim red night lights). Bundle it with REM sleep in a 'sleep upgrades' carousel.
candidates.why_now: Yahoo Health and other syndication are recycling it this week. Works well alongside the REM content.

evidence.signal: This nightly habit could be changing the structure of your heart

candidates.topic: 'Don't toss cannabis leaves: rare compounds with medical potential'
candidates.angle: Not recommended: lab chemistry only, with no human evidence. Any coverage would invite claims about unproven cannabis treatments.
candidates.why_now: ScienceDaily press release on Sep 25; hype-bait headline.

evidence.signal: Lab compound discovery, no clinical data
